title: The Incident Response Cycle, Planning, and Exercises
objective: By the end of this lesson you can walk through the IR phases, explain what IR planning must contain, describe exercise types from tabletop to full-scale, and apply the idea of testing AI-integrated defenses.

blocks.text: Incident response is a cycle, not a one-way pipeline. The widely taught phases (consistent with NIST guidance) run: preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication, and recovery; and post-incident activity, with communication running throughout. Expanded for memory:

items: Preparation: plans, playbooks, tools, contacts, training, and logging in place before anything happens. Most of your IR capability is bought here.
Detection and analysis: alerts and reports are triaged (previous lesson) and the incident is confirmed and scoped.
Containment: stop the spread, short-term (isolate hosts, block domains, disable accounts) and long-term (apply fixes so it cannot repeat immediately).
Eradication: remove the adversary's foothold, malware, accounts, and persistence mechanisms.
Recovery: restore from clean backups, verify integrity, monitor closely as systems return to service.
Post-incident (lessons learned): blameless review within days, while memory is fresh; update playbooks, detections, and controls.

blocks.text: Exam sequencing traps: containment precedes eradication (stop the bleeding, then remove the cause), and lessons learned is a phase, not an afterthought. Evidence handling matters throughout: preserve logs and images before cleanup destroys them.

items: Roles and contact chains: who leads, who decides, who speaks publicly, reachable at 3 a.m.
Severity definitions and escalation criteria, agreed before the crisis.
Playbooks for expected incident types (phishing, ransomware, data exposure) with concrete first steps.
Communication plans: internal, legal, regulators, customers, and out-of-band channels if primary systems are down.
Legal and evidence guidelines: what to preserve, chain of custody basics, when to call counsel.

rows: Discussion-based: the team talks through a scenario and injects, following the plan; finds gaps cheaply
Practice one procedure, such as restoring one backup or calling the notification chain
Teams respond in a simulated environment

blocks.text: Start tabletop, graduate upward: a tabletop that reveals nobody knows the contact chain has paid for itself many times over. Every exercise ends with an after-action review and tracked improvements, or it was theater.

The 2026 outline adds testing of AI-integrated defenses to D5. The principle: if an AI system participates in your defenses (SIEM AI ranking alerts, AI-powered IPS blocking, AI phishing filters), it is part of the attack surface and part of the exercise plan. Test that AI-assisted detections actually fire on realistic samples, that blocking actions do not take down legitimate business flows, that analysts know how to challenge a wrong AI verdict, and that the response plan covers the AI vendor or service failing. Fold AI components into tabletop scenarios explicitly, so teams rehearse the human-plus-machine decisions they will actually face.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Order: prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, lessons learned. Isolate before eradicating; preserve evidence before cleanup. Tabletop = cheap discussion-based gap finder. AI-assisted defenses get exercised like any other control.

blocks.title: Phase a ransomware story
steps: Phase each event: (1) EDR flags encryption behavior on a file server; (2) the server is network-isolated; (3) backups are verified clean and tested; (4) systems are rebuilt and restored; (5) a review updates the playbook and email gateway rules.
Name the phase where most damage is limited or lost.
Add one tabletop inject involving the AI-assisted email filter that missed the delivery.
blocks.expected: 1: detection and analysis. 2: containment. 3-4: eradication and recovery. 5: post-incident lessons learned. Damage is decided at containment speed. Inject example: 'the phishing email passed the AI filter with high confidence; adjust and retest the filter, and update the playbook's report path.'

blocks.description: Drag six shuffled incident response phases back into the order a real incident runs through, from preparation to lessons learned. Full design: labs/ir-sequence-order.lab.en.md.

cheatsheet: IR phases: preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, lessons learned; communication throughout.
Contain before you eradicate; preserve evidence before cleanup.
IR plan = roles and contacts, severity and escalation, playbooks, communications, legal/evidence guidance.
Exercises: tabletop (talk-through, cheap) > drill > functional > full-scale; always close with tracked improvements.
AI-integrated defenses are exercised too: verify detections fire, blocking is safe, analysts can challenge AI verdicts.

checkpoint.prompt: Malware is confirmed on one workstation. Which action belongs to the containment phase?

choices.C: Network-isolating the machine and disabling the affected credentials

checkpoint.explanation: Containment stops the spread right now: isolate hosts, block indicators, disable compromised accounts. Training updates belong to preparation or post-incident follow-up.

checkpoint.prompt: An organization wants to test its incident response plan for the first time with minimal cost and disruption. The best starting choice is:

choices.A: A tabletop exercise discussing a scenario against the plan
choices.B: A full-scale live simulation in production

checkpoint.explanation: A tabletop is discussion-based, cheap, non-disruptive, and reliably exposes gaps in roles, contacts, and procedures. Full-scale comes later; real incidents are not a test plan.
